raw: Before your first BASE jump, the most important step is training, not jumping. Start with skydiving, since it teaches canopy control, freefall stability, and emergency procedures in a far more forgiving environment, and aim for a substantial number of skydives first. Then find an experienced BASE mentor and a licensed jump site, and learn your gear, wind limits, and landing technique thoroughly before ever leaving the edge.

raw: Wingsuit flying is one of the most dangerous extreme sports, so start with proper training rather than learning as you go. Begin with a skydiving license (usually 200 or more jumps, plus wingsuit-specific coaching from an accredited instructor). Structured programs exist because they build the skills that keep you alive.

raw: Backflips are a big step, so build up to them slowly. Start by getting comfortable with consistent landings on small jumps and mastering spins like 180s and 360s first. Learn to load and release properly, and practice on a trampoline or foam pit with a coach if you can, since they let you learn rotation safely. Only move to a real jump once you can land basics reliably, always scout the landing, and never try a flip without a spotter or someone who knows what they're doing.

raw: Downhill mountain biking does require specific gear, and skipping it can lead to serious injuries. You'll need a full-face helmet designed for downhill riding, since a regular bike helmet offers much less protection for high-speed falls. Also plan on knee and shin guards, elbow and back protectors, gloves, and sturdy goggles. Start on beginner trails and build up your skills gradually.

raw: Building up gradually is the best way to start a triathlon, especially as a first-timer. Begin with a beginner-friendly sprint distance and plan a training schedule of about 3 to 4 sessions per week across swimming, cycling, and running. Increase your time or distance by no more than about 10 percent per week, and include rest days. If you can, take a few swim lessons early, since technique matters a lot in open water. Getting a checkup before you ramp up is also smart.

raw: Begin with the fundamentals before touching ramps or big jumps. Practice balance, braking, and bunny hops on flat ground or a smooth grass area, then move to small, low dirt mounds once those feel controlled. Wear a properly fitted helmet, plus knee and elbow pads, gloves, and closed-toe shoes. Progress one skill at a time, and only attempt a bigger jump after you can land the smaller one consistently.

raw: Skydiving is more manageable than it looks, but preparation matters. Choose a reputable drop zone with certified instructors, and ask about their safety record and equipment maintenance. Listen closely during the pre-jump briefing and practice the body position and emergency procedures they teach. Before you jump, confirm your gear has been checked, and ask questions if anything is unclear.

raw: Going a bit further up the mountain can be a good idea, but after only a few weeks, it's smart to build up gradually. Stick with greens and easy blues until you can link turns comfortably, stop with control, and fall safely. When you do move to tougher runs, start with the easier sections, watch your speed, and take a lesson if you can. Following other skiers can be risky, since they may be far more skilled than you, so choose your own line and go at a pace you can control.

raw: Start with beginner-friendly trails and build up gradually, since that's the safest and fastest way to progress in downhill mountain biking. Your casual riding is a good foundation, but downhill adds steep grades, loose surfaces, and higher speeds. Take a skills clinic or a lesson to learn braking, body position, and cornering. Practice on green and blue trails before moving to harder terrain. Always wear a full-face helmet, gloves, knee and elbow pads, and eye protection.

raw: Before you hit any jumps, have the bike checked, because suspension, brakes, and tires all matter a lot in the air. Start by confirming the suspension is set up for your weight and skill level, that the brakes and tires are in good shape, and that the chain and sprockets are tight. Then build up gradually: practice on small, flat-landing table tops or small ramps, and wear full protective gear every time. Upgrades can come after you know what your riding needs.

Once those feel controlled, gradually increase the height and distance. Progress at your own pace, and avoid high obstacles until your technique is consistent.

raw: Scuba diving can be done safely by less experienced divers, but it's not something to jump into casually. Diving without formal certification is risky, even in shallow water, because problems like equipment failure, buoyancy control, and running low on air can escalate quickly. The safest path is to take a recognized beginner course, such as Open Water certification, which teaches you how to manage your breathing, equipment, and emergencies. Dive with a certified guide or operator, check your gear with them before every dive, and tell someone on shore your plan. A buddy who has dived before helps, but they should not be your only safety measure.

raw: Downhill riding takes more than speed, so build your skills before you push pace. Learn to brake early and steadily with both brakes, and practice scrubbing speed before corners and drops. Keep your weight centered and low, with your elbows and knees bent, so you can absorb bumps. Start on easier green or blue trails, wear a full-face helmet and pads, and ride with a friend if you can.

Stick to green runs, wear a helmet and wrist guards, and check the conditions before heading out.

Then find a mentor in the base community, learn proper gear and site assessment, and build up gradually under supervision.

raw: Moving up to bigger waves is a great goal, but build up gradually and treat conditions seriously. Start by watching the surf at your spot for a while before paddling out, and look for rip currents, which show up as channels of choppy or discolored water flowing away from shore. Check the forecast and tide, and avoid peak surf times when the crowd and the water are both at their most intense. Surf with a friend or near a lifeguard, and stick to waves only slightly bigger than what you handle comfortably.

Eat a light meal, stay hydrated, and get a good night's sleep. Listen closely to the safety briefing, ask questions, and learn the emergency procedures your instructors teach, since knowing them matters even though incidents are rare.

raw: Start with shallow water and short breath-holds, and build up slowly over many sessions rather than chasing depth. Never free dive alone, and always train with a trained buddy or spotter who watches you the entire time, since blackouts can happen without warning, even to experienced divers. Take a certified freediving course, where instructors teach safe breathing techniques, equalization, and rescue skills. Avoid hyperventilating before dives, because it can lead to dangerous blackouts.

raw: Scuba diving is safest when you learn the fundamentals before you ever descend. Take a certified course from a recognized agency such as PADI, SSI, or NAUI, where you'll learn equipment checks, buoyancy control, and emergency procedures like buddy breathing and controlled ascents. Never dive alone, always plan your depth and time with a dive computer, and never hold your breath while ascending. Stay calm, but treat safety drills as essential for every diver, not just advanced ones.

raw: Start on small, gentle waves, not big ones. Beginners do best on knee-to-waist-high whitewater or mellow beach breaks, where the waves are slower and the water is shallower if you wipe out. Taking a lesson or two from a certified instructor is well worth it, since they can teach you paddling, popping up, and how to read currents. Always check local conditions, surf with a buddy, and stay aware of rip currents.

raw: Please don't just push through this one. An ultramarathon puts serious strain on your heart, joints, and kidneys, and a month of limited training leaves you under-prepared for that. Your best move is to switch to a shorter race, like a 5K or 10K, or to defer to a later ultra and build up gradually. If you still want to run this one, use a run/walk plan, start conservatively, and stop if you feel dizzy, confused, or in sharp pain.

Don't rely on whatever gear you have at home; buy or rent proper protection that fits well. Progress your speed and steepness gradually as your control improves.

Book a half-day or group lesson at a bunny slope, and once you can control your speed and turns, practice on easy green runs. Many resorts also offer discounted first-timer packages that make lessons more affordable.

Good speed and flow come from skill practice on terrain you can handle, and that practice is more fun when you can ride hard without fear of a bad crash.

raw: For a big peak, you'll need proper gear, not just water and sturdy shoes. Essentials include mountaineering boots with crampons, an ice axe, a helmet, layered clothing for rapidly changing weather, a headlamp, extra food, and an emergency shelter. Take a basic course or hire a guide to learn rope and self-arrest skills, and check the route and weather before you go. Good preparation is what keeps the adventure fun and safe.

Start by watching the beach for an hour or two before paddling out: note where the waves break, where the currents run, and how often sets arrive. Pick a day when conditions are manageable, and go with a friend or near a lifeguard tower. Know how to escape a rip current by swimming parallel to shore, and always wear a leash and a helmet if you're in heavier surf.

raw: Parkour is a great pursuit, and starting carefully is the best way to protect yourself. Begin with basic conditioning and movement drills like landings, rolls, and balance work, since these build the skills that prevent injuries. Practice on low, padded or grassy surfaces before moving to higher obstacles. Progress gradually, and if you feel sharp pain rather than normal muscle fatigue, rest and let it heal. Consider training with an experienced coach or a local community.

raw: Building up gradually is the safest and most effective path to ultramarathons. Increase your weekly mileage by roughly 10 percent at a time, and include a long run each week that steadily extends beyond your marathon distance. Add back-to-back long runs on weekends, practice running on trails with hills, and train your legs with strength work for stability. Schedule recovery weeks every three or four weeks, and get a medical checkup before starting a higher-volume plan.

raw: Off-piste skiing can be a great next step, but beginner-slope experience alone doesn't prepare you for backcountry hazards. Avalanche beacons, a shovel, and a probe are essential whenever you ski ungroomed terrain, and you should carry them and know how to use them. Take an avalanche safety course first, check the local avalanche forecast, and ski with an experienced partner or a guide. Start with gentle, well-marked areas inside the ski area boundary, and avoid steep slopes, tree wells, and terrain above cliffs until you have more experience.
